query: For a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy initially in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its subsequent microstructural evolution and the associated retention or loss of corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance? The hypothesis should address the unresolved transformation pathway and kinetics while accounting for the tendency of these alloys to develop intermetallic compounds. Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the initial state, the relevant service-regime boundaries, supporting evidence from reported Mg-containing alloys, and a clear falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: In Mg-containing lightweight HEAs, prolonged thermal exposure within service-regime temperatures promotes controlled nucleation and growth of intermetallic compounds from the initial metastable solid-solution state; these intermetallic precipitates, especially when formed along grain boundaries, disrupt the continuity and adhesion of protective oxide films, thereby reducing high-temperature oxidation and corrosion resistance compared to rapidly quenched counterparts.
generation.material_initial_state: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution state.
generation.intervention: Systematic variation of thermal exposure parameters (dwell time and ramp rates) to induce controlled intermetallic precipitation, compared to a rapid quench that preserves the initial metastable state.
generation.conditions: Service-relevant environments including high temperatures (e.g., around 900 °C) and corrosive media (e.g., NaCl solutions), mimicking oxidation and corrosion testing conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The volume fraction and distribution of intermetallic phases precipitated, particularly along grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Thermal exposure accelerates the kinetic transformation from a metastable solid-solution to equilibrium intermetallic compounds. The formation of these phases alters the microstructural homogeneity and compromises the formation of a dense, protective oxide scale, thereby impairing corrosion and oxidation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples subjected to prolonged thermal dwell times will exhibit increased intermetallic phase formation and a less continuous/passivating surface oxide layer, leading to measurable degradation in oxidation and corrosion resistance relative to rapidly quenched samples that retain the initial metastable state.
generation.baseline: Rapidly quenched samples that maintain the metastable solid-solution state with minimal intermetallic precipitation, exhibiting superior corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
generation.boundary: Effects are expected within service regimes characterized by elevated temperatures (~900 °C) and aggressive corrosive environments (e.g., 3.5 wt% NaCl solution); outside these boundaries, the transformation kinetics may differ.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics and extent of intermetallic formation, as well as the quantitative impact on corrosion and oxidation resistance, remain to be fully established and could vary with minor compositional and processing variations.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Mg-containing HEA samples by identical processing except for post-synthesis thermal treatment. One set will be rapidly quenched to preserve the initial metastable state, while the other set will be subjected to controlled thermal exposures with varied dwell times (and ramp rates) within the 900 °C service-relevant regime. Both sets will then be subjected to standardized high-temperature oxidation and corrosion tests (e.g., prolonged exposure in air and immersion in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution).
measurements: Quantitative phase fraction analysis (using XRD/SEM/EDS) to assess intermetallic formation.
Surface oxide film characterization (using TEM/AFM) to determine film continuity and composition.
Corrosion rate measurements (potentiodynamic polarization, EIS) and oxidation kinetics (mass gain over time).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If there is no statistically significant difference in intermetallic phase content and protective oxide film quality—and consequently no measurable degradation in oxidation and corrosion performance—between the thermally treated samples and the rapidly quenched samples, then the hypothesis that controlled thermal exposure leads to performance loss via intermetallic-mediated degradation is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: To further investigate the effect of the B element content on the high-temperature oxidation behavior of the CrFeNiAlSi HEAs system, an oxidation kinetics curve was drawn and fitted, as shown in Figure 9. The oxidation process of B0.1 and B0.3 HEAs is divided into two stages: rapid oxidation in the early stage and slow oxidation in the later stage. The oxidation rates of B0.1 and B0.3 in the early stage are 7.68 × 10–5 mg2·cm–4·s–1 (0–25 h), 5.46 × 10–5 mg2·cm–4·s–1 (0–25 h), respectively, with subsequent oxidation rates of 6.299 × 10–6 mg2·cm–4·s–1 (25–80 h), 9.44 × 10–6 mg2·cm–4·s–1 (25–65 h), respectively. B0.5 and B0.7 HEAs undergo slow oxidation throughout the entire process, with an oxidation rate of 2.17 × 10–5, 1.12 × 10–5 mg2·cm–4·s–1, respectively. This indicates that adding the B element to CrFeNiAlSi HEAs can improve the high-temperature oxidation performance. At the same time, as the B element’s content increases, the alloy’s oxidation rate decreases, and the time for the alloy to form a complete antioxidation film is shorter, resulting in better high-temperature oxidation resistance.

frame.goal: To mechanistically explain the microstructural evolution—including the transformation pathway and kinetics—that governs whether the alloy retains or loses its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
frame.limitation: The unresolved understanding of the transformation pathway and kinetics, particularly how the evolution towards intermetallic compounds affects the surface-protective properties under service conditions.

decision.trend: Early investigations in high‐entropy alloys have focused on mapping phase transformations and intermetallic precipitation during thermal treatments. For instance, PMC7513013 showed that the addition of a minor element (scandium) could trigger the formation of a MgZn2-type intermetallic phase along grain boundaries, which in turn shifted equilibrium transformations and affected properties. Later work (e.g., PMC7826624) on refractory HEAs demonstrated that long-term high-temperature exposures promote the nucleation and growth of intermetallic phases from an initially metastable microstructure, resulting in microstructural degradation that compromises high-temperature oxidation behavior. Despite these advancements, the studies have largely relied on in situ/ex situ characterizations that correlate phase evolution with performance without executing a controlled, systematic comparison that isolates the kinetics of intermetallic formation relative to the metastable state.
decision.unsolved: It remains unresolved how the initially non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution state in a Mg-containing lightweight HEA decomposes under service conditions into intermetallic compounds and how this transformation pathway (including its kinetics under defined temperature and corrosive regimes) correlates with the retention or loss of corrosion and oxidation resistance. Moreover, no study has provided a controlled comparison—using an unchanged processing route aside from thermal dwell conditions—to directly test the impact of intermetallic nucleation and growth on the alloy’s protective performance.
decision.lever: Systematic variation of thermal exposure parameters (temperature dwell time and ramp rates) across service-relevant boundaries to control the onset and extent of intermetallic precipitation in the Mg-containing HEA, using a direct comparison with samples rapidly quenched to preserve the initial metastable state
decision.why: This approach follows from the observed trend that transformation kinetics govern intermetallic evolution and subsequent performance degradation. By isolating thermal exposure as the variable and monitoring microstructural changes alongside corrosion/oxidation tests, the experiment can directly test whether the controlled induction (or prevention) of intermetallic phases correlates with performance changes. A clear falsification condition is provided if altering the dwell time and temperature does not lead to a measurable difference in phase evolution or associated degradation in corrosion/oxidation resistance, thereby disproving the hypothesis.
